title: Refraction: why light bends in water and lenses

summary.text: A straight pencil in a glass of water looks snapped at the water line. This happens because light bends when it passes at a slant from water into air. This bending is called refraction, and it happens because light travels more slowly in water and glass than in air. A lens is a curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light on purpose, and a magnifying glass uses it to make small things look bigger. Water drops, marbles and the lens inside your own eye bend light in the same way. The air around the Earth bends sunlight too, so we still see the Sun for about two minutes after it has set.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a straight pencil in a steel tumbler of water that looks snapped at the water line, on the right a child's eye huge behind a magnifying glass held over an ant.

intro.hook: Put a pencil in a glass of water and look at it from the side. It looks snapped in two at the water line. Pull it out. It is whole. So which do you believe, your eyes or your hands?
intro.text: About two thousand years ago, a Roman writer called Seneca noticed something odd. Small letters looked bigger and clearer when he read them through a glass ball filled with water. People who fish with spears know another puzzle. Fish are not quite where they look, and a spear thrown straight at them passes above them. In this unit you will find out what happens to light at the edge of water and glass, and why it causes both of these surprises.
intro.art: A steel tumbler of water on a kitchen table with a pencil that looks broken at the surface, and a child's hand pulling a whole pencil out of it.

outcomes: I can say what refraction is: light bending as it goes from one see-through material into another, like from water into air.
I can explain why a pencil in water looks broken or bent, even though it is really straight.
I can run a fair test with water drops, changing only the size of the drop, and say which drop makes letters look biggest.
I can explain that a magnifying glass makes things look bigger, but does not make them bigger, because it bends the light coming from them.
I can finish an experiment like a scientist: what I think, what I saw, and why.
I can name lenses in my life: spectacles, cameras, water drops and the lens inside my own eye.

I can describe big examples of bending light: seeing the Sun after it has set, archerfish that aim correctly in spite of the bend, and galaxies whose light is bent by gravity. I can also say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: What lets us see. Light comes from things like the Sun or a lamp, bounces off things, and travels into our eyes.
terms.example: In a dark room you can see nothing. Switch on the tube light and you see everything.
terms.art: A tube light shining on a cup, with an arrow from the cup to a child's eye.

terms.meaning: A material that lets light pass straight through it, so you can see things on the other side. Scientists call it transparent.
terms.example: Clear water, a glass tumbler and a clean window are see-through.
terms.art: A clear glass of water with a flower clearly visible behind it.

terms.meaning: Light bending as it goes at a slant from one see-through material into another. It bends right at the edge where the two meet. When light bends like this, we say it refracts.
terms.example: A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looks broken at the top of the drink. That is refraction.
terms.art: A straw in a glass of lemonade, looking snapped at the surface, with a bent light arrow drawn at the edge.

terms.meaning: To change direction. Light usually travels in straight lines. When light bends, it changes direction at one place and then travels straight again.
terms.example: A car going straight that turns at a corner, then goes straight again.
terms.art: A straight arrow that turns at a dotted line and carries on straight in a new direction.

terms.meaning: The outside edge of something, where it meets something else. The top of water in a glass is the water's surface.
terms.example: When you look at a pond, the shiny top you see is its surface.
terms.art: A glass of water with its top surface glowing.

terms.meaning: A piece of see-through material with a curved shape, made to bend light in a useful way.
terms.example: Spectacles, a camera and a magnifying glass all have lenses.
terms.art: A round glass lens seen from the side, thick in the middle and thin at the edges.

terms.meaning: A lens with a handle, which makes things look bigger when you hold it near them. It is also called a hand lens.
terms.example: A watch repairer in the market holds a small magnifying lens against one eye to see tiny parts.
terms.art: A magnifying glass held over a newspaper, with one word looking huge.

terms.meaning: To make something look bigger than it is. The thing itself stays the same size.
terms.example: Through a magnifying glass, an ant looks as big as your thumb. The ant has not grown.
terms.art: An ant seen normally beside the same ant looking big through a lens.

terms.meaning: A lens that is fatter in the middle than at its edges. Scientists call it a convex lens. It bends light inwards, and it can magnify.
terms.example: A magnifying glass and a glass marble are both bulging lenses.
terms.art: Side view of a bulging lens with three arrows going in and bending towards each other.

terms.meaning: A picture of a thing made by light, which is not the thing itself. You can see an image through a lens, or catch one on a wall.
terms.example: A magnifying glass can throw a small upside-down image of a window onto a sheet of paper.
terms.art: A magnifying glass throwing a tiny upside-down picture of a bright window onto white paper.

terms.meaning: To bring light together so a picture looks sharp, not blurry. You focus a magnifying glass by moving it nearer or further.
terms.example: When you move a lens until the letters stop being blurry, you have focused it.
terms.art: Two views through a lens: blurry letters, then sharp letters.

terms.meaning: Two lenses in a frame, worn in front of the eyes, to help people see clearly. They bend light a little before it enters the eye.
terms.example: Many grandparents wear reading spectacles to read the newspaper.
terms.art: A pair of spectacles resting on an open newspaper.

terms.meaning: A small clear lens inside your eye, just behind the pupil, the dark hole in the middle of your eye. It helps bend light to make a sharp picture inside your eye.
terms.example: Your eye lens changes shape a little when you look at something near, then something far.
terms.art: A simple side view of an eye with a small bean-shaped lens inside, labelled with a pointing hand.

terms.meaning: A tool with very strong lenses that makes tiny things look hundreds of times bigger.
terms.example: With a microscope you can see the tiny living things in a drop of pond water.
terms.art: A simple microscope with a drop of pond water on a glass slide, and tiny swimming creatures shown in a circle.

terms.meaning: The blanket of air around the Earth. Light from the Sun and stars passes through it to reach us.
terms.example: When you look at the sky, you are looking through the atmosphere.
terms.art: The Earth with a thin glowing layer of air around it, and sunlight entering it.

terms.meaning: The force that pulls every object towards every other object. The heavier the object, the stronger its pull.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a mango down from a tree. Gravity also holds the Moon near the Earth.
terms.art: A mango falling from a tree with a downward arrow.

terms.meaning: A huge cluster of galaxies, or another very heavy thing in space, whose gravity bends light from galaxies far behind it. It works like a giant lens.
terms.example: Space telescopes have photographed far galaxies stretched into bright arcs and rings by a gravitational lens.
terms.art: A cluster of yellow galaxies with blue arcs of light curving around it.

terms.meaning: A drawing, a toy or an act-out that helps explain something we cannot easily see.
terms.example: Marching in a line from tiles onto a mattress is a model of light bending.
terms.art: Children holding hands in a line, turning as they step from a tiled floor onto a mattress.

explanations.definition: Refraction is light bending as it goes at a slant from one see-through material into another, for example from water into air. The bend happens right at the edge where the two materials meet.
explanations.description: In one material, like air, light travels in straight lines. When it reaches water or glass at a slant, it changes direction at the edge. We say the light refracts. Then it goes straight again in its new direction. If light hits the water straight on, at a right angle, it does not bend at all. It only bends when it arrives at a slant.
examples: A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looks broken at the top of the drink.
Your legs look short and stumpy when you stand in a clear pool or a river.
A coin at the bottom of a bucket of water looks closer to the top than it really is.
explanations.art: A torch beam going down through air, bending at the water's surface in a glass tank, and carrying on straight in a new direction.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what refraction, the bending of light, is.

explanations.concept: Why a pencil in water looks broken
explanations.definition: A pencil in water looks broken because light from the part under water bends as it leaves the water. Our eyes think the light came in a straight line, so we see that part in the wrong place.
explanations.description: You see the pencil because light from it comes into your eyes. Light from the top part, in the air, comes straight to you. Light from the bottom part starts in the water. At the water's surface, or at the side of the glass, it bends. Your eyes and brain do not know about the bend. They follow the light straight back, as if it had never turned. So they see the underwater part a little higher, or a little to one side, of where it really is. The two parts do not line up, and the pencil looks snapped. Your hand feels the truth, because the pencil itself never changed.
examples: A spoon in a glass of water looks broken and fatter under the water.
An oar dipped in a river looks bent at the water line.
Fish in a pond are a little lower and further away than they look.
explanations.art: A pencil in a glass, with a dotted line showing where the eye thinks the bottom is, and a solid bent line showing the real path of the light.
explanations.context: This card explains the broken-pencil trick, where a straight pencil in a glass of water looks snapped at the water line.

explanations.concept: Water looks shallower than it is
explanations.definition: Because light bends as it leaves water, the bottom of a bucket, a tank or a pool looks closer to the top than it really is. Seen from straight above, water looks about three quarters as deep as it really is. From a slant, it looks even shallower.
explanations.description: Light from a coin at the bottom of a bucket bends as it comes out of the water. Your eyes follow that light straight back, and they see the coin higher up than it is. This is why a coin hidden by the side of a cup can suddenly appear when you pour water in. It is also why ponds, tanks, wells and swimming pools are deeper than they look. Never jump into water because it looks shallow.
examples: A coin hidden behind the edge of a cup appears when water is poured in.
Steps going down into a temple tank look shorter under the water.
A swimming pool 4 feet deep looks only about 3 feet deep when you look straight down into it.
explanations.art: A child on the edge of a temple tank seeing the bottom step higher than it really is, with a dotted line showing where it seems to be.
explanations.context: This card explains why water looks less deep than it really is, and why that matters for staying safe near ponds and pools.

explanations.concept: Why light bends: it slows down
explanations.definition: Light bends because it travels more slowly in water and glass than in air. When one side of a beam slows down first, the beam turns.
explanations.description: Light is the fastest thing there is. But it does go a little slower inside water, and slower still inside glass. In water, light goes about three quarters as fast as in air. In glass, it goes about two thirds as fast. Picture a line of children holding hands and marching across a tiled floor. They march onto a soft mattress at a slant. The child who reaches the mattress first slows down first. The others are still marching fast. So the whole line swings round and changes direction. Light does the same at the edge of water or glass. If the line walks onto the mattress straight on, everyone slows at the same moment, and nobody turns.
examples: A toy car rolled at a slant from a tiled floor onto a carpet turns as its first wheel hits the carpet.
A line of marching children turns as they step at a slant from the road onto sand.
Light going into a glass block bends, and bends back again when it comes out the other side.
explanations.art: A line of children holding hands, marching at a slant from shiny tiles onto a soft mattress, with the line swinging round.
explanations.context: This card explains the reason light bends at the edge of water or glass: it slows down there.

explanations.concept: How a magnifying glass makes things look big
explanations.definition: A magnifying glass is a bulging lens. It bends the light from a small thing so that the light reaches your eye as if it came from a bigger thing. So your eyes see a bigger picture. The thing itself does not grow.
explanations.description: A magnifying glass is fatter in the middle than at its edges. Light going through it bends towards the middle, twice: once going in and once coming out. When you hold it close over a small thing, like an ant or a word, the bent light reaches your eye as if it came from a much bigger ant or word. So your eye sees a big picture, called an image. Move the lens slowly away from the thing, and the image grows bigger. Move it too far, and the image goes blurry. Further still, and the world through it turns small and upside down. The ant never changes. Only the path of the light changes.
examples: A watch-repair woman wears a small lens in her eye to see tiny screws.
Grandparents' reading spectacles for close work are bulging lenses that make letters look bigger.
Doctors look at a cut or a splinter through a lens.
explanations.art: Side view: an ant, a bulging lens and an eye, with light lines from the ant bending in the lens, and a faint, much bigger ant drawn where the eye thinks the light came from.
explanations.context: This card explains how a magnifying glass, a hand lens, makes small things look big by bending light.

explanations.concept: A lens can throw a picture onto a wall
explanations.definition: A bulging lens can bring light from a bright scene together onto a wall or a sheet of paper. It makes a small, sharp, upside-down picture there, called an image.
explanations.description: Stand across the room from a bright window. Hold a magnifying glass between the window and a sheet of white paper. Move the lens slowly towards the paper and away. At one place, a tiny picture of the window appears on the paper. It is upside down, and if a tree is outside, you might even see the tree. The lens takes the light spreading out from each point of the window and brings it back together at one point on the paper. Light from the top of the window lands at the bottom, so the picture is upside down. A camera works in the same way. So does your eye, which makes a tiny upside-down picture at its back. Your brain sorts it out, so you see the world the right way up.
examples: A phone camera has tiny lenses that throw a picture onto a light sensor inside it.
In an old cinema, a lens threw the film's picture, very big, onto the screen.
Never look at the Sun through a lens. A lens brings sunlight together into a spot hot enough to burn paper, and it can blind an eye.
explanations.art: A magnifying glass held up, throwing a tiny upside-down image of a window with a tree onto a sheet of white paper.
explanations.context: This card explains how a magnifying glass can make a picture of a window on a sheet of paper, the way a camera does.

explanations.concept: Water drops, marbles and bottles are lenses too
explanations.definition: Any rounded, see-through thing can bend light like a lens. A water drop, a glass marble and a round bottle of water all magnify. The smaller and rounder the drop, the more it magnifies.
explanations.description: A drop of water on a leaf is round on top, like a tiny bulging lens. So the leaf under it looks bigger. A small, very round drop bends light more sharply than a big, flat puddle, so it magnifies more. About 350 years ago, a cloth seller in Delft, in the Netherlands, called Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made tiny, very curved glass lenses, some smaller than a peppercorn. Some of his microscopes made things look more than 200 times bigger. With them he became one of the first people to see bacteria, tiny living things in drops of water and in his own mouth. He described them in letters, from 1676 onwards. A round water bottle standing up is curved only from side to side. So it bends light only sideways, and writing behind it looks wide, not big all over.
examples: A drop of water on a leaf makes the tiny veins under it look bigger.
A glass marble placed on a newspaper makes the letters under it look big.
A water bottle held in front of a word makes the word look stretched sideways.
explanations.art: Close-up of round dew drops on a green leaf, with the leaf's veins looking bigger inside each drop.
explanations.context: This card explains that water drops, marbles and round bottles of water bend light and magnify, like a magnifying glass.

explanations.concept: Inside the glass: light and electrons
explanations.definition: Light slows down in glass and water because it makes the tiny electrons in their atoms jiggle. The jiggling electrons send out light of their own. Together, the old light and the new light travel more slowly through the material.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, far too small to see. Each atom has even tinier parts called electrons. Light is a ripple of electricity and magnetism travelling through space. When light passes through glass, its ripple makes the electrons in the glass jiggle back and forth. Each jiggling electron sends out a tiny ripple of light too. All these ripples add up with the light going in. The result is light that moves through the glass more slowly than through air. Air has far fewer atoms packed into each spoonful than glass does, so light in air is only slowed a very tiny bit. This is a simple picture of something physicists describe with careful maths.
examples: Diamond slows light more than glass does, to less than half its speed in air.
Air slows light only a tiny bit, so light bends only a little when it goes from empty space into air.
Hot air and cold air slow light by slightly different amounts. That is why the air above a hot road shimmers.
explanations.art: A zoom-in circle on a glass block, showing a wavy light ripple passing among dots for atoms, each with a tiny jiggling electron sending out small ripples.
explanations.context: This card zooms right in, to the atoms inside glass and water, to see why light slows down there.

explanations.concept: The sky bends sunlight: seeing the Sun after it has set
explanations.definition: The Earth's air bends sunlight downwards a little, around the curve of the Earth. So at sunset, you still see the whole Sun for about two minutes after it has really gone below the horizon.
explanations.description: The air is denser near the ground and thinner high up. So light coming in from space bends a little as it passes down through the air, the atmosphere. At sunset and sunrise, the Sun's light comes in very low and at a big slant, and bends the most. The bend lifts the Sun's picture up by about the Sun's own width. So when the bottom of the Sun seems to touch the horizon, the real Sun is already just below it. We see each sunrise a couple of minutes early and each sunset a couple of minutes late. Every day is a few minutes longer than it would be without air. The bend is also why the setting Sun often looks squashed, flatter at the bottom.
examples: A sunset over the sea at Kanyakumari looks squashed, flatter at the bottom, because the lowest part is bent the most.
Stars near the horizon look a little higher than they really are.
Stars twinkle because moving air bends their light this way and that, very quickly.
explanations.art: The Earth's curve with a layer of air, a real Sun just below the horizon, and a bent light line making it appear just above, to a child on a beach.
explanations.context: This card is about a huge example of refraction: the air around the Earth bending sunlight, so we see the Sun after it has set.

explanations.concept: Gravity bends light too: lenses in space
explanations.definition: Huge masses, like a giant cluster of galaxies, bend light that passes near them. This is not refraction through glass. It happens because gravity curves space, and light follows the curve. But it works like a giant lens.
explanations.description: In 1915, Albert Einstein worked out that gravity bends the paths of light. Light passing close to the Sun should bend a tiny amount. In 1919, during a total eclipse of the Sun, two teams of astronomers photographed stars near the darkened Sun. One team was on the island of Principe, off Africa, with Arthur Eddington. The other was in Sobral, in Brazil. The stars appeared slightly out of place, about as much as Einstein had said. Today space telescopes photograph whole clusters of galaxies that bend light from galaxies far behind them. The far galaxies look stretched into bright arcs, and sometimes into a full ring. Priyamvada Natarajan, an astrophysicist born in Coimbatore, measures these bends. From them she maps dark matter, invisible matter whose gravity bends the light.
examples: The 1919 eclipse photographs showed stars near the Sun slightly out of place.
Pictures from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes show far galaxies bent into arcs around nearer clusters.
Looking at a torch through the thick round foot of a wine glass makes rings and arcs that look like gravitational lenses.
explanations.art: A cluster of glowing yellow galaxies with thin blue arcs of a far galaxy curving around it like a broken ring.
explanations.context: This card goes out into space: gravity from huge clusters of galaxies bends light, like a giant lens.

explanations.concept: Living lenses: eyes, fish and archerfish
explanations.definition: Animal eyes use lenses to bend light into a sharp picture. Animals that hunt across the water's surface have ways to deal with the bend.
explanations.description: The clear front of your eye, the cornea, does most of the bending. The lens inside your eye does the fine focusing, by getting fatter or thinner. Under water, the cornea hardly bends light, because the eye and the water slow light by about the same amount. So fish have almost perfectly round lenses, which bend light strongly. The four-eyed fish of South America swims with their eyes half in and half out of the water. Each eye has two pupils, one looking up into the air and one looking down into the water. Each lens is shaped like an egg, so it can focus both views at once. The archerfish, found in mangroves including the Sundarbans, spits a jet of water at insects on leaves above the water. Scientists found that they aim correctly even though the bend at the surface moves the insect's picture. Pied kingfishers often hover and then dive almost straight down. Seen from straight above, the fish is right below where they seem to be, only a little deeper.
examples: When you go swimming without goggles, everything looks blurry. Your cornea cannot bend light properly when water touches it.
An archerfish can knock an insect off a leaf with a jet of water from below the surface.
A kingfisher on a wire over a paddy field dives almost straight down onto a fish.
explanations.art: An archerfish under the water's surface spitting a thin jet at a beetle on a mangrove leaf, with a dotted line showing where the beetle looks to be.
explanations.context: This card is about lenses in living things, and how animals that hunt across water deal with the bend.

explanations.concept: Who first found the rule of bending?
explanations.description: Light bends by a definite amount, depending on the slant and the materials. Finding the exact rule took many hundreds of years. Who gets the credit is still argued about.
examples: Many science books call it Snell's law, after Willebrord Snell.
In France it is often called Descartes' law.
Historians found the same rule in a book by Ibn Sahl, from about 984.

perspectives.who: Claudius Ptolemy, a scientist in Alexandria, Egypt, about 1,850 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He carefully measured how much light bends going from air into water and glass, at many slants. He wrote the numbers in tables. His numbers were close, but his rule was not quite right.

perspectives.who: Ibn Sahl, a mathematician in Baghdad, in his book On Burning Mirrors and Lenses, about 984
perspectives.explanation: He used the correct rule of bending to design curved lenses that bring light to a point. The historian Roshdi Rashed found this in 1990. Many historians now say Ibn Sahl found the rule first, more than 600 years before Europe.

perspectives.who: Willebrord Snell in the Netherlands, 1621, and René Descartes in France, 1637
perspectives.explanation: Snell found the rule but did not publish it. Descartes published it in 1637. In much of the world it is still called Snell's law.

perspectives.who: Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in Cairo, in his Book of Optics, written about 1011 to 1021
perspectives.explanation: He did careful experiments on bending light through water and glass, and studied how a glass ball magnifies. He insisted that ideas must be tested by experiments, a habit at the heart of science.

explanations.art: Four small portraits in a row, with a pencil-in-water drawing in the middle: an old Greek scholar, a scholar in Baghdad with a lens drawing, a scholar in Cairo, and a Dutchman with a measuring tool.
explanations.context: This card is about the history of the rule that says how much light bends, and the argument about who found it first.

explanations.concept: Does light push water forwards or backwards?
explanations.description: Light carries a tiny push. Sunlight pressing on a huge, thin sail in space can push a spacecraft. But what happens to light's push when it goes into water or glass? Scientists argued about this for about a hundred years.
examples: Japan's spacecraft IKAROS, launched in 2010, sailed using the push of sunlight on a huge thin sail.
Experiments have shone strong light onto water and watched whether the surface bulges in or out.
Every time light bends in a lens, the lens gets a tiny push too small to feel.

perspectives.explanation: His maths said light's push gets bigger when it enters water or glass.
His maths said light's push gets smaller when it enters water or glass.

perspectives.who: Stephen Barnett, a physicist in Scotland, 2010
perspectives.explanation: He argued that both were right, about two different kinds of push. Many physicists agree, but experiments are still being done, and some still argue.

explanations.art: A beam of light entering a tank of water, with a question mark over two arrows on the water's surface, one pointing in and one pointing out.
explanations.context: This card is about a real puzzle inside refraction that scientists argued about for a hundred years.

explanations.concept: Bending light the wrong way, and invisibility cloaks
explanations.description: All ordinary materials bend light to the same side. In 1967, the Russian physicist Victor Veselago asked what would happen if a material bent light the opposite way. Nobody had seen one. Around the year 2000, John Pendry in London worked out how to build one from tiny metal shapes. David Smith and his team in California then built it. It worked only for microwaves, a kind of invisible light. In 2006, a team at Duke University in the USA hid a small copper cylinder from microwaves, bending them smoothly around it like water around a rock. A cloak that hides a person from ordinary light is still only an idea. It may never work fully.
examples: A cloak made in 2006 hid a small copper cylinder from microwaves, but not from our eyes.
Some scientists use special materials to make lenses that see finer details than ordinary lenses can.
Other teams have made small cloaks that hide tiny objects from ordinary light, but only when seen from certain directions.
explanations.art: Light lines flowing smoothly around a small cylinder, like water flowing around a rock in a stream.
explanations.context: This card is about the frontier: scientists building new materials that bend light in strange ways, maybe even to hide things.

agreed.text: Light bends when it goes at a slant from one see-through material into another.
agreed.evidence: In a dark room, shine a torch at a slant into a glass of water with a few drops of milk in it. The milk makes the beam show up in the water. The beam goes down more steeply than the torch is pointing. People have measured this bend for nearly 2,000 years.

agreed.text: A pencil in water only looks broken. It does not really bend.
agreed.evidence: Feel it under the water, or pull it out. It is straight. Look from straight above, and the break almost vanishes.

agreed.text: Light travels more slowly in water and glass than in air.
agreed.evidence: In 1850, Léon Foucault in Paris compared light going through a tube of water with light going through air. It was slower in the water. Hippolyte Fizeau and Louis Breguet found the same that year.

agreed.text: A bulging lens makes things look bigger when it is held close to them, and it can make an upside-down picture on a wall.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with a magnifying glass, a newspaper and a bright window.

agreed.text: Gravity bends light passing near huge masses.
agreed.evidence: The 1919 eclipse photographs showed stars near the Sun slightly out of place. Space telescopes now photograph many galaxies bent into arcs and rings.

challenging.claim: A pencil in water really bends, because the water pushes it.
challenging.who: Most of us, at first. Many children and adults think this when they first see it.
challenging.for: It really does look bent, every time, and from almost every side.
challenging.against: Feel it under the water. It is straight. Pull it out. It is straight. Look from straight above, and it looks almost straight. Only the light changes direction, not the pencil.
challenging.context: This card is about a common first idea about the broken-pencil trick, and why it is wrong.

challenging.claim: A magnifying glass makes things bigger.
challenging.who: Many young children, and the way we often talk: 'it makes the ant bigger'.
challenging.for: Through the lens, the ant really looks bigger.
challenging.against: Measure the ant with a ruler without the lens. Then look again with the lens. The ant has not changed. Lift the lens away and the ant looks small again at once. Only the path of the light changes.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea about magnifying glasses.

challenging.claim: Light always travels in straight lines, so nothing can change its path.
challenging.who: A common rule people learn first, and over-use.
challenging.for: In one material, like air, light does go in straight lines. That is why a shadow has the shape of the thing that makes it.
challenging.against: Light goes straight inside one material. But at the edge of water or glass, it changes direction. Huge masses in space bend it too.
challenging.context: This card is about the rule that light goes in straight lines, and where it stops being true.

challenging.claim: The Nimrud lens, a polished piece of rock crystal about 2,700 years old, was used as a magnifying glass, or even in a telescope.
challenging.who: Some historians, including Giovanni Pettinato, an Italian expert on ancient Iraq, in 1999.
challenging.for: It was found in 1850 by Austen Henry Layard in the ruins of a palace at Nimrud, in Iraq. It is shaped a little like a lens, and it does magnify a little.
challenging.against: Many experts think it was a decoration, an inlay for furniture. Its shape is uneven and its magnifying is weak and blurry.
challenging.context: This card is about a very old piece of crystal and whether people used it as a lens.

challenging.claim: The rule of how much light bends was first found by Ibn Sahl in Baghdad, around 984, not by Snell in 1621.
challenging.who: The historian Roshdi Rashed, who found Ibn Sahl's work in 1990.
challenging.for: Ibn Sahl's book, On Burning Mirrors and Lenses, uses the correct rule to design lenses.

story.title: The Kingfisher Who Kept Missing
story.note: Pied kingfishers are real. They live across India, and they really do hover over water and dive almost straight down. Fishers really do learn to aim below where a fish appears. The kingfisher Chhaya, the girl Mitali, her grandmother and everything that happens to them are made up. Scientists are still studying how much diving birds learn about the bend, and how much they are born knowing.
text: I am a pied kingfisher, black and white like a page of writing, and I was the worst fisher on the whole river.

My mother could hang in the air above the water as if the sky were holding her up by a thread. Her wings would whirr. Her head would stay perfectly still. Then she would fold up like a closed umbrella and drop, straight down, plop, and come up with a silver fish crosswise in her beak. She did it again and again, all morning, while I sat on the electric wire above the ferry ghat and watched.

My name is Chhaya. It means shadow. I think my mother chose it because I was always close behind her. But that summer, the summer I had to learn to feed myself, I did not feel like her shadow. I felt like her opposite.

Here is what I did. I sat on the wire, low over the water, where I could see the fish quite well. I chose one. The fish hung there, close to the top, slow and silver, so easy. I looked at them with both eyes and I dived, a long, beautiful slanting dive, like an arrow from a bow.

And I hit the water, and I opened my beak, and there was nothing. Every time. The fish was always a little lower than I aimed, and a little further away. They would flick their tail and vanish into the green. I would come up with water up my nose and river weed on my head, and the crows on the bank would laugh their ugly laugh.

On the ghat steps below my wire, a girl came every morning with her grandmother. The girl was called Mitali, and she had a small net on a bamboo pole. The grandmother had a very old basket and very sharp eyes. They fished for little puti fish for the evening curry. And I saw that Mitali missed too.
She would see a fish, swing her net at them, and catch only water. She stamped her foot on the wet step. 'They move,' she said. 'They see me coming and they move.'
Her grandmother laughed, not unkindly. 'They do not move, Mitali. They were never there.'
Mitali stared at her. I stared too, from my wire.

The grandmother took the stick she used for walking and pushed one end into the water, at a slant. 'Look at my stick,' she said. Mitali looked. So did I. The stick was broken. Right at the top of the water, it bent, like a knee. The part under the water pointed somewhere new.
The grandmother pulled it out. It was straight. She put it in again. Broken. Out. Straight.

'The water bends the light,' she said, 'not the stick. Light comes up out of the water and turns a little corner at the top. Your eyes do not know about the corner. They think the light came straight. So they show you the stick in the wrong place. And the fish in the wrong place.'
'Then how do you ever catch anything?' said Mitali.

'Two ways,' said the grandmother. 'When you are looking at a slant, aim lower than the fish, below where they seem to be. Your hands learn it, slowly. Or else...' and she leaned right out over the step, and looked down, straight down, at her own feet in the water. 'Look from straight above. When you look straight down, the light comes straight up and does not turn its corner. The fish is right below you, where they seem to be, only a little deeper.'

She stood the stick upright in the water, right under her eyes. 'Come and look from here,' she said. Mitali leaned over and looked straight down along it. This time it did not look broken at all. It went into the water like a finger into milk, straight all the way.
I almost fell off my wire.

Straight down. My mother never dived from the wire. She never slanted like an arrow. She climbed up into the air, high over the fish, and she hung there, whirring, until she was right above them. And then she dropped straight down, along the one path where the river cannot tell lies.
I had thought her hovering was showing off. It was the whole secret.

The next morning I did not sit on the wire. I flew out over the deep water and I tried to hover. It is very hard. You must beat your wings fast enough to stay still, which sounds impossible, but it is not. I wobbled. I sank. I flapped harder and rose too high. The crows laughed. Mitali, on the step, pointed up at me and laughed too, but it was a different laugh. Her grandmother shaded her eyes and watched me.

At last I found the trick of it. The wind came up the river, and I leaned into it, and my head stayed still. Below me, a fish hung in the green. I did not dive at a slant. I waited until I was right above them. Then I folded, and dropped, straight as a stone down a well.
Cold water. A flick of silver. And then a weight in my beak, wriggling, real.
I flew back to the wire with my first fish. I banged my fish on the wire, the way my mother does, and I gulped them down. It was the best meal I have ever eaten, and it was very small.

On the step below, Mitali was standing very still, right on the edge, looking straight down at her feet. She lowered her net slowly, straight down, upright, beside her toes. When she lifted the net, a puti fish was jumping inside, bright as a coin.
Her grandmother did not say anything. She just tapped her stick twice on the step.

Mitali looked up at me. I looked down at her. We had both learned the same thing in the same morning, and neither of us could have told the other about it. Then she laughed, and I flew up into the wind to hover again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the fish is never where they seem to be when you look at a slant, because light bends as it leaves the water. Your eyes follow the light straight back and see the fish higher and nearer than they really are. But light that leaves the water straight up does not bend. So looking from straight above, the fish is right below where they seem to be, only a little deeper. This may be one reason pied kingfishers hover and dive almost straight down. The grandmother's stick shows refraction: it looks broken when you look at it at a slant, and straight when you look down along it from above. The story also quietly honours knowledge carried by ordinary people, like a grandmother who fishes, long before anyone wrote it down.
ask: Why did Chhaya keep missing the fish when she dived from the wire at a slant?
What happened to the grandmother's stick when she pushed it into the water at a slant? And when she pushed it in straight down?
Why was the mother kingfisher's hovering 'the whole secret'?
The grandmother knew about bending light without ever going to school for it. Where else do people know something from doing it, before anyone explains it?
Chhaya and Mitali learned the same thing in the same morning. Can a bird and a girl really learn the same lesson?

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: is light being bent here, so things look moved or broken? Is it being bent to make things look bigger? Or is light not bending at all? Put the card on the BENT, BIG or NEITHER mat.
Then say why, using the word 'bend' or 'straight'. A good reason wins one lens token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. The first person to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

options: BENT
BIG
NEITHER
check.why: Light from the part of the straw in the drink bends as it comes out at the top. Your eyes see that part in the wrong place, so the straw looks broken. That is BENT. Picking NEITHER usually means thinking the straw itself is bent. Picking BIG is close, because the straw can look a little fatter too, but the main thing is the break.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it and puts it on a mat. 2. They say why, using 'bend' or 'straight'. 3. Give one token for each good reason.

flow.parent: Tricky cards: the shadow, the face in a steel plate and the torch beam are NEITHER. A shadow is light blocked, and a steel plate bounces light back. Those belong to other units. Twinkling stars and the squashed Sun are BENT, by the air. The camera, microscope, spectacles, dew drop, marble, bottle and watch-repair lens are BIG, though the camera makes a small picture. The coin, the fish, the legs in the pool and the temple tank are BENT. The kingfisher card can go on BENT or NEITHER if the reason is good: they dive straight down, where the bend cannot fool them. items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, stands a steel spoon in a glass of water. From the side, the handle looks broken at the water line. What is really bent?
opts: The spoon
The path of the light coming from the spoon
The glass
Nothing. Her eyes are tired.
items.why: The spoon stays straight, and she can feel that with her finger. Light from the part under the water bends as it comes out into the air. Her eyes follow the light straight back, so they show that part in the wrong place. A strong answer says the light bent, not the spoon.

items.p: When light goes at a slant from water into air, it changes direction. This bending of light is called ____.
items.why: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one see-through material into another, like water into air. It happens right at the edge where the two meet.

items.p: Kavya wants the pencil in her glass of water to look as straight as possible. Where should she put her eye?
opts: Low down at the side, looking at a slant
Straight above the glass, looking down along the pencil
Anywhere. It looks broken from everywhere.
items.why: Light that comes straight up out of the water hardly bends. So from straight above, the break almost vanishes. At a slant the light bends the most, so the pencil looks most broken. A strong answer links where you look to how much the light bends.

items.p: Many people think the water really bends a pencil a little, the way hot water bends a plastic straw. True or false: the pencil in the water is really bent.
items.why: False. Run a finger along the pencil under the water: it is straight. Pull it out: still straight. Only the light from it changed direction. A strong answer gives the touch test as evidence.

items.p: In the broken-pencil test, your eyes told you the pencil was broken. What did you do to check, and what did you find?
items.a: I felt along the pencil under the water and it was straight. I pulled it out and it was whole. I looked from straight above and it looked almost straight. So the pencil was never broken. Only the light from it bent.
items.why: A strong answer uses the child's own test: at least one check that is not just looking from the side, and what it showed.

items.p: Lakshmi puts a coin in an empty cup and moves her head back until the rim just hides the coin. She keeps her head still while her sister slowly pours in water. What will Lakshmi see?
opts: Nothing changes. The coin stays hidden.
The coin comes into view over the rim.
The coin looks smaller and sinks lower.
items.why: Light from the coin bends as it leaves the water, to a flatter slant. Now it can pass over the rim and reach her eye. The coin has not moved, but it looks higher than it is. A strong answer says the light bent, not the coin moving.

items.p: Sort these moments. Is light being bent as it passes through water, glass or a lens, or not?
items: your legs look short in a swimming pool
Light bends
a dew drop makes a leaf's veins look big
Light bends
your hand makes a shadow on the wall
Light does not bend
Paati's reading spectacles make letters clear
Light bends
a torch beam goes straight across a dark room
Light does not bend
a round fish bowl makes the goldfish look fat
Light bends
items.a: see items
items.why: Light bends when it passes at a slant through water, glass or a lens. A shadow is light being blocked, and a torch beam in plain air goes straight. A strong sorter asks: is the light passing from one see-through material into another?

items.p: Divya puts two drops of water on a clear ruler lying on a newspaper. One is a tiny round drop. One is a big flat puddle. Which drop will make the letters look bigger?
opts: The big flat puddle, because it has more water
The tiny round drop, because it is more curved
Both the same, because water is water
items.why: It is the curve that matters, not how much water there is. A tiny drop is very round on top, so it bends light the most and magnifies the most. Many children first guess the big puddle. The test shows the opposite.

items.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 4, looks at an ant through a magnifying glass. She says, 'My lens made the ant grow.' What is wrong with what she said?
opts: Nothing. The ant grew while she looked.
The ant stayed the same size. The lens bends the light from the ant, so the ant looks bigger.
The lens pulled the ant closer to her.
items.why: Take the lens away and the ant looks small again at once. Nothing about the ant changed. Only the path of the light changed. A strong answer says 'looks bigger', not 'is bigger'.

items.p: A magnifying glass is a lens that is fatter in the ____ than at its edges.
items.why: A bulging lens, fatter in the middle, bends light inwards. That is what makes things look bigger through it. A flat window hardly changes how things look.

items.p: All of these are lenses. Match each lens to the job it does.
pairs: the lens inside your eye
makes a sharp picture at the back of your eye
spectacles
bend light before it enters the eye, so the picture is sharp
a magnifying glass
makes a small thing look bigger
a phone camera lens
makes a small picture of the world on the camera chip
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every lens is a curved, see-through piece that bends light on purpose. Each one bends light to do a different job.

items.p: Put the steps of the broken-pencil test in order, from first to last.
items: Stand a pencil in an empty glass and look at it
Pour in water up to half way
Look from the side, from a slant and from straight above
Feel the pencil under the water
Say what I think, what I saw and why
items.why: First see the pencil straight with no water, so you have something to compare with. Then add water and look from three places. Then check with touch. Last, explain like a scientist.

items.p: Draw a pencil leaning in a glass of water, and your eye above the glass, off to one side. Draw a dotted line for the light going from the bottom of the pencil to your eye.
items.a: The dotted line goes up through the water at a slant. At the water's surface it bends to a new direction, then goes straight to the eye. The pencil looks broken at the water line.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the bend in the light line exactly at the surface, where water meets air, and keeps the pencil itself straight.
items.art: An empty glass outline with a water line, and an eye above it and to one side.

items.p: After the broken-pencil test, three people in one family argue about how to find out whether the pencil is really bent.

views.says: Trust your eyes. I can see it is broken.
Trust your hands. My finger felt it straight all the way down.
Look again from straight above. Then you need no hands, and your eyes tell the truth.

items.ask: Which way would you trust most to find out? Give a reason from your own test. Then say one good point that another person makes.
items.a: A strong answer picks one way and backs it with what the child saw or felt. For example, the hand is good because touch is not fooled by bending light. It then admits a fair point from another side: hands can be fooled too, for example by very cold water, and looking from above is a real check with the eyes. The best answers say that using two checks is better than one.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Eyes can be fooled by bending light, but they are still useful when you look from the right place. Scientists check with more than one sense and more than one test.

items.p: A temple tank looks shallow from the steps. Why can it be deeper than it looks? Why does this matter?
items.a: Light from the bottom of the tank bends as it leaves the water. My eyes follow the bent light back and see the bottom higher than it really is. Water often looks only about three quarters as deep as it is. So someone who jumps in thinking it is shallow could be in danger.
items.why: A strong answer explains the bending and gives the safety point: never judge water depth by eye.

items.p: In the March Like Light act-out, a line of people marched from the floor onto a mattress at a slant. Why did the line turn?
opts: The mattress pushed them sideways
The person at one end stepped on first and slowed down first, so the line swung round
Everyone got tired at the same moment
items.why: One end of the line slowed down before the other end. The fast end kept going and swung round the slow end. Light does the same at the edge of water, because one side of a beam slows down first. A strong answer says 'slowed first'.

items.p: Revathi shines a torch straight down into a bucket of water, at a right angle to the surface. What does the beam do as it goes into the water?
opts: It bends a lot
It goes on straight, only a little slower
It all bounces back up
items.why: Straight on, the whole beam reaches the water at the same moment and slows down together, so nothing makes it turn. It is like the marching line stepping onto the mattress all at once. Bending needs a slant.

items.p: Light slows down more in glass than in water. Imagine a straw standing half in a tub of solid clear glass instead of water. Would the break look bigger or smaller? Explain why.
items.a: Bigger. Light slows down more in glass, so it turns more sharply at the edge. More turning means the hidden part looks more out of place, so the break looks bigger.
items.why: A strong answer links more slowing to more bending, and more bending to a bigger break. It uses the slowing idea to predict, not just to describe.

items.p: Selvi stands on the bank of a pond with a net. She sees a fish at a slant through the water. Where should she aim the net?
opts: Exactly at the fish she sees
A little below where the fish seems to be
A little above where the fish seems to be
items.why: The light coming from the fish bends at the surface, so the fish looks higher and nearer than they really are. The real fish is lower and further away. A strong answer aims below the picture, because the picture is lifted.

items.p: Three hunters catch fish that they see through the water. Each has a different way to deal with the bend in the light.

views.who: Selvi's grandmother, who fishes from the ghat steps
views.says: Stand on the bank and aim lower than the fish seems to be. Your hands learn how much, with practice.
Hover high over the fish, then drop straight down. Light coming straight up does not bend, so the fish is right below.

views.who: An archerfish, a fish who hunts insects
views.says: Stay under the water and aim at the insect above. You learn to allow for the bend, from below.

items.ask: Which way do you think works best for a person on the bank? Give a reason from what you learned about bending light. Then say one thing another hunter's way does better.
items.a: A strong answer picks a way and explains it with bending light. For example, the grandmother's way works from the bank, but the right amount to aim lower changes with the slant and the depth, so it takes practice. It then gives a fair point for another way: looking straight down removes the bend completely, but a person cannot hover. The best answers see that each way fits the hunter's body and place.
items.why: There is no single winner. Each hunter has a real trade-off between how easy the way is and how well it removes the bend.

items.p: A magnifying glass held between a bright window and a sheet of white paper can make a small picture of the window on the paper. The picture is upside ____.
items.why: The lens brings light from the top of the window down to the bottom of the picture, and light from the bottom up to the top. So the picture is upside down, as in a camera.

items.p: A big round water bottle magnifies more strongly than a small glass marble, because the bottle holds much more.
items.why: False. The small marble is much more curved, so it bends light more sharply and magnifies more. The curve decides how strongly a lens magnifies, not the amount of glass or water.

items.p: When you open your eyes under water without goggles, everything looks blurry. Why? And why do goggles make it clear again?
items.a: The clear front of my eye does most of the bending, but only when light comes into it from air. Water and my eye slow light by nearly the same amount, so in water the light hardly bends there, and the picture is blurry. Goggles put a pocket of air in front of my eyes, so the bending works again.
items.why: A strong answer says that bending needs a change in how fast light goes, and that goggles bring back the air.

items.p: Some animals hunt across the surface of water. Match each animal to how they deal with bending light.
pairs: pied kingfisher
hovers and dives almost straight down
archerfish
aims a jet of water correctly at insects above the surface
four-eyed fish
has eyes that look into the air and the water at the same time
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Animals that hunt across the surface have found different ways around the bend.

items.p: Put these lenses in order, from the weakest magnifier to the strongest.
items: A flat window pane
A big round water bottle
A glass marble
A tiny drop of water in a hole in foil
items.why: The more curved the lens, the more sharply it bends light, and the stronger it magnifies. A flat pane has no curve. A tiny drop is the most curved of all, which is why Leeuwenhoek's microscopes used tiny lenses.

items.p: At Kanyakumari, when the bottom of the setting Sun seems to touch the sea, the real Sun is already just below the horizon.
items.why: True. The air bends the Sun's light downwards around the curve of the Earth, so the Sun looks a little higher than it really is. We still see the Sun for about two minutes after it has really set.

items.p: Ishita, a girl in Class 4, says, 'Light bends in water because water is heavy and pulls the light down.' What is wrong with her idea? What really makes light bend?
items.a: Water does not pull light down. Light goes into water from below, from the side and upwards out of it, and it bends every way. What really happens is that light goes slower in water. At a slant, one side of the beam slows first, so the beam turns.
items.why: A strong answer finds the mistake (a pull) and gives the real cause (slowing down at a slant). Bonus: light coming up out of water bends too, which a downward pull cannot explain.

items.p: Draw the March Like Light act-out seen from above. Show the floor, the edge of the mattress and the line of people turning. Add arrows for where they walk.
items.a: The line walks at a slant towards the mattress. The first person to step on slows down. The line swings round and walks on in a new direction, closer to straight across the edge.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the turn happening at the edge, and the slower side being the one that stepped on first.
items.art: An empty rectangle split by a line into 'floor' and 'mattress' halves.

items.p: Priya's reading spectacles make the words in her book look bigger. What shape are her lenses?
opts: Fatter in the middle than at the edges
Thinner in the middle than at the edges
Flat, like a window
items.why: Lenses that make things look bigger are bulging lenses, fatter in the middle, like a magnifying glass. A flat lens would not change the words. A lens thinner in the middle makes things look smaller.

items.p: In the bottle-lens activity, words seen through a round bottle lying on its side looked stretched up and down, but not side to side. Use the shape of the bottle to explain why.
items.a: The bottle is curved up and down, round its middle, but it is straight along its length. Light only bends where there is a curve. So the words are stretched only in the direction the bottle curves.
items.why: A strong answer connects the curve to the direction of magnifying: no curve, no bending.

items.p: Light goes about three quarters as fast in water as in air, about two thirds as fast in glass, and less than half as fast in diamond. Which bends light the most when light goes into it from air at a slant?
opts: Water
Glass
Diamond
items.why: The more a material slows light, the more sharply light turns at its edge. Diamond slows light the most, so it bends light the most. That is part of why diamonds sparkle. A strong answer uses the speeds, not a guess about hardness.

items.p: Imagine light went at exactly the same speed in water as in air. Predict what you would see in the broken-pencil test. Explain why.
items.a: The pencil would look straight, because nothing would make the light turn at the surface. With no change in speed, there is no bending. The water itself would also be very hard to see.
items.why: A strong answer uses the cause of bending (a change in speed) to predict a new case. Bonus: we see the edge of clear water partly because light bends there.

items.p: More than 300 years ago, two famous scientists explained bending light in opposite ways.

views.who: Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, about 1690
views.says: Light is a wave. Waves slow down in water, so they turn, like marchers stepping onto sand.

views.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in 1704
views.says: Light is a stream of tiny particles. Water pulls them in as they enter, so light goes faster in water, and that pull turns it.

items.ask: Imagine it is the year 1800 and nobody has timed light in water yet. Which idea would you back, and why? What test would settle it? Then say why the other idea was sensible too.
items.a: A strong answer picks one idea and gives a reason, for example that the marching act-out shows how slowing makes a line turn. It names the deciding test: time light in water and in air. It explains the other side fairly: Newton's idea also explained the bending, and he was very famous. It may add that in 1850 Léon Foucault timed light in water and found it slower, so Huygens was right about the speed.
items.why: Both ideas explained the bend, but they made opposite guesses about speed. That is what made a test able to decide. Most scientists followed Newton for about a hundred years, which shows that fame is not evidence.

items.p: In 1919, during a total eclipse of the Sun, astronomers photographed stars that were close to the darkened Sun in the sky. What did they find?
opts: The stars were exactly where they always are
The stars looked slightly out of place, because the Sun's gravity bent their light
The stars had disappeared
items.why: Albert Einstein had predicted in 1915 that gravity bends the path of light. The photos showed the stars shifted by about the amount he predicted. This is not refraction through a material. It is gravity bending light.

items.p: When a torch shines through the round foot of a wine glass from exactly behind its middle, the light spreads into a bright ____.
items.why: A round lens bends light evenly on every side, so light from exactly behind it becomes a ring. Space telescopes see the same shape, an Einstein ring, when a far galaxy is exactly behind a huge one.

items.p: The setting Sun often looks squashed, flatter at the bottom than at the top. Use what you know about bending light to explain why.
items.a: The air bends sunlight downwards, and it bends light from low in the sky the most. The bottom of the Sun is lowest, so its light is lifted more than the light from the top. The bottom is pushed up towards the top, so the Sun looks squashed.
items.why: A strong answer says the bending is not the same for every part of the Sun, and that light from lower down passes through more air at a bigger slant.

items.p: An archerfish is under the water. She looks up at a beetle sitting on a leaf above the pond. To her, where does the beetle seem to be?
opts: Exactly where the beetle really is
Higher above the water than the beetle really is
Lower, closer to the water, than the beetle really is
items.why: The bend works both ways. To us on the bank, a fish looks lifted towards the surface. To a fish looking up, a beetle in the air looks lifted further from the surface. Scientists found that archerfish still aim correctly, so they allow for the bend.

items.p: The Nimrud lens is a polished piece of rock crystal, about 2,700 years old, found in Iraq. Some experts say people used it to magnify. Others say it was only a decoration. What evidence could help you decide?
items.a: I could check whether it is shaped evenly, like a good lens, and how clearly it magnifies. I could look for old writings or pictures of people using lenses at that time. I could check whether other lenses were found in the same place.
items.why: A strong answer suggests evidence, not opinions. Experts still disagree about this.

items.p: Draw a cup with a coin stuck at the bottom, and your eye just too low to see the coin over the rim. Then draw water in the cup, and the path of light from the coin to your eye.
items.a: Without water, the straight line from coin to eye hits the rim. With water, the light goes up from the coin through the water. At the surface it bends to a flatter slant, passes over the rim and reaches the eye.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the bend at the water's surface and shows that the coin has not moved.
items.art: Outline of a cup from the side, with a coin at the bottom and an eye beside the rim.

items.p: In the drop-microscope project, why does a tiny drop of water in a hole in foil magnify far more than a big magnifying glass?
opts: The tiny drop is much more curved, so it bends light more sharply
Water is a better material than glass
The foil adds its own light
items.why: A tiny drop is almost a full ball, very curved. The more curved the lens, the more sharply it bends light and the more it magnifies. Leeuwenhoek's tiny glass beads worked the same way.

items.p: Stars twinkle because moving pockets of warm and cool air bend their light a little this way and that. Would stars twinkle for an astronaut standing on the Moon?
opts: Yes, more than on Earth
No, because the Moon has no air to bend the starlight
Only on full-moon nights
items.why: Twinkling is caused by air. The Moon has almost no air, so starlight comes straight through and the stars shine steadily. A strong answer uses the cause to predict the new case.

items.p: Match each real person to what they found out about bending light.
pairs: Ibn Sahl, in Baghdad, about 984
used the correct rule of bending to design lenses
Ibn al-Haytham, in Cairo, about 1011 to 1021
tested bending light with experiments and studied how a glass ball magnifies
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, in Delft, from the 1670s
made tiny bead microscopes and saw bacteria
Priyamvada Natarajan, born in Coimbatore
maps invisible dark matter from how it bends light
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: People in many lands, over a thousand years, worked out how light bends and how to use it.
items.context: This question is about people from the history and the frontier of bending light.

items.p: Name another time, outside this unit's tests, when your eyes could be fooled because light bends. How would you check what is really there?
items.a: For example: my feet look close to the top when I stand in a pool, or the road far ahead looks wet on a hot day. I could check by touching, by measuring with a stick, or by looking from straight above or walking closer.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real example of bending light and a check that does not rely on the same view. That is how science tests the senses.

items.p: Light can change direction in different ways. Sort each moment by what changes the light's path.
cats: Bent by passing into another material
items: a straw looks broken in a glass of nimbu pani
Bent by passing into another material
a far galaxy looks stretched into an arc
Bent by gravity
you see your face in a steel plate
Bounced back
the air above a hot road shimmers
Bent by passing into another material
stars near the eclipsed Sun look shifted
Bent by gravity
the Moon shines with sunlight
Bounced back
items.a: see items
items.why: Refraction is bending as light passes into a different material, like water, glass or warmer air. Gravity bends light near huge masses. Bouncing back is reflection. A strong sorter asks what the light passed through or near.

items.p: From straight above, water looks only about three quarters as deep as it really is. A temple tank looks 90 centimetres deep. About how deep is it really? Show how you worked it out.
items.a: About 120 centimetres. 90 is three quarters of the real depth, so one quarter is 90 divided by 3, which is 30. Four quarters is 4 times 30, which is 120 centimetres. That is deeper than many children are tall.
items.why: A strong answer reasons with the fraction backwards, from the part to the whole, and notices why it matters for safety.

items.p: Everything about light inside water is settled, and scientists no longer argue about any of it.
items.why: False. How light bends is very well understood. But scientists argued for about a hundred years about what happens to light's push inside water. Hermann Minkowski in 1908 and Max Abraham in 1909 gave different answers. Some still argue about it today.

experiments.title: The Broken Pencil: is it really bent?
experiments.question: Does a pencil in water really bend, or does it only look bent? And does where you look from change how broken it looks?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the pencil look broken from the side? From a slant? From straight above? Will it feel broken if you touch it under the water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same glass, the same pencil and the same amount of water each time. Only change one thing: where you look from. Then change only the liquid: no water, then water.
results_table: Glass of water: broken or straight?
How big was the jump? (none, small, big)

materials.item: a clear glass tumbler, or a clear plastic bottle with the top cut off by a grown-up
a pencil, or a straw, or a steel spoon
water, to fill the glass about three quarters full
a second pencil, to fill in the results table

experiments.safety: If you use a glass tumbler, keep it in the middle of the table so it cannot be knocked off. Wipe up spills, so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Look at a pencil in an empty glass, then in a glass of water, from the side, from a slant and from straight above. Feel it under the water. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the pencil as it looked from the side, and as it really is.

flow.do: 1. Put an empty clear glass on the table. 2. Stand a pencil in it, leaning against the side. 3. Ask your child to look from the side, at the level of the glass.
flow.say: Here is a pencil in an empty glass. Look at it from the side. Is it straight or broken?
flow.kid: Put a pencil in an empty glass. Let it lean. Look from the side. Is it straight?
flow.context: This is the first step of the broken-pencil test. You find out whether a pencil in water really bends, or only looks bent.

good: It looks straight.
It looks normal, the same as outside the glass.

flow.do: 1. Without moving the pencil, pour water into the glass until it is about three quarters full. 2. Ask your child to guess first, before looking.
flow.say: Now I'll pour in water. Before you look, guess. Will the pencil still look straight?
flow.kid: Now pour water into the glass, about three quarters full. Guess first. Will the pencil still look straight?

flow.do: 1. Look from the side, at the level of the water. 2. Then look from a little above, at a slant. 3. Then look from straight above, down into the glass. 4. Write each result in the table.
flow.say: Look from the side. Now from a slant. Now straight down from the top. Where does the pencil look most broken?
flow.kid: Look from the side. Then from a slant. Then straight down from the top. Where does it look most broken? Write it in the table.
flow.parent: From the side, through the curved glass, the underwater part often looks fatter and jumps sideways. From a slant above the water, it looks bent upwards at the surface. From straight above, the break almost disappears. All three results are interesting. There is no wrong result.

check.q: In the broken-pencil test, where did the pencil look least broken?
options: From the side
From a slant
From straight above
check.why: Light coming straight up out of the water hardly bends, so from straight above the pencil looks almost straight. From a slant, the light leaves the water at a slant and bends the most. If you picked 'from the side', look again. The side of a round glass also bends light, so the pencil often jumps sideways there.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put a finger into the water and run it down the pencil. 2. Then pull the pencil out and look at it.
flow.say: Run your finger down the pencil, under the water. Does it feel broken? Now pull it out. Is it broken?
flow.kid: Put your finger in the water. Feel the pencil all the way down. Does it feel broken? Now pull it out and look.

ask.q: Your eyes said broken. Your finger said straight. Which was right?
good: My finger, because the pencil is straight when I pull it out.
The pencil is straight. It only looks broken in the water.

flow.think: If your eyes can be fooled by water, how else might they be fooled?

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw two pictures. 2. First, the pencil as it looked from the side. 3. Second, the pencil as it really is. 4. Then add a dotted line for the path of the light, from the bottom of the pencil to the eye.
flow.say: Let's draw a model, a picture that explains. Draw the pencil as it looked. Then draw it as it really is. Draw how you think the light travels from the bottom of the pencil to your eye.
flow.kid: Draw two pictures. The pencil as it looked. The pencil as it really is. Then draw the light going from the pencil to your eye.
flow.parent: A good drawing shows the light going straight in the water, bending at the surface, and going straight to the eye. The eye then 'sees' the pencil along that last straight line, too high. Do not correct the drawing yet. The explanation cards come next.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the pencil does not really bend. It only looks broken. What I saw: in the water it looked broken, most from a slant and least from straight above. But it felt straight, and it was straight when I pulled it out. Why: the light from the underwater part bends at the top of the water, and my eyes think it came straight.

experiments.context: This is the broken-pencil test. You put a pencil in a glass, add water, and look from different places. Then you feel it, to find out if it really bends.

experiments.title: The Water-Drop Magnifier: which drop makes letters biggest?
experiments.question: Does a small drop of water or a big drop of water make letters look bigger?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will a tiny drop, a medium drop or a big drop make the letters under it look biggest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, put all three drops on the same clear ruler, lying on the same newspaper. Only change the size of the drop. Make fresh drops and look 3 times, because one look can be a fluke.
results_table: Try 1: how much bigger did the letters look?
About how many times taller (1, 1 and a half, or 2)

materials.item: a clear plastic ruler, the see-through kind from a school geometry box, or a clear plastic box lid
a page of newspaper with small print
a toothpick and a straw, to make drops
a cup of water
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Water and plastic only. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make a tiny, a medium and a big drop on a clear ruler lying on newspaper. Compare how big the letters look under each drop, 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the tiny, medium and big drop. Then draw a bar for each drop, as tall as how many times taller it made the letters look.

flow.do: 1. Lay the newspaper flat on the table. 2. Lay the clear ruler on a line of small print. 3. Fill a cup with water.
flow.say: We're going to make lenses out of water. First, lay this clear ruler on the newspaper, over a line of small letters.
flow.kid: Lay the newspaper flat. Put the clear ruler on a line of small letters.
flow.context: This is the first step of the water-drop magnifier test. You make drops of different sizes and find out which one makes things look biggest.
flow.parent: The ruler holds each drop about 2 millimetres above the letters. That small gap lets a tiny drop magnify well. If the drops soak into paper, they stop being lenses, so always put them on the plastic.

flow.do: 1. Dip the tip of a toothpick in the water and touch it to the ruler. This leaves one tiny drop, about the size of a mustard seed. 2. Dip a straw in the water and put a finger over its top end. Lift your finger a little to let out one drop the size of a pea. 3. Let out several drops in one place to make a big drop, as wide as a one-rupee coin. Keep the drops well apart along the ruler.
flow.say: Let's make three drops. A tiny one like a mustard seed, a medium one like a pea, and a big one like a coin. Which do you think will make the letters look biggest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make three drops on the ruler. One tiny, like a mustard seed. One like a pea. One big, like a coin. Guess first.

ask.q: Why did you choose that drop?
good: The big one, because it has more water.
The tiny one, because it is rounder.

flow.parent: Most children guess the big drop, because it has more water. That is a good guess to test. Write the guess and the reason down before you look.

flow.do: 1. Look straight down through each drop, one at a time. 2. Compare a letter inside the drop with the same size of letter just beside it. 3. Decide: does it look the same, a bit bigger, or about twice as tall? 4. Write it in the table. 5. Wipe the ruler, make three fresh drops and look again. Do this 3 times.
flow.say: Look through the tiny drop. Now look at the letters just beside it. Does the letter inside look the same, a bit bigger, or twice as tall?
flow.kid: Look through each drop. Look at the letters beside it too. Which look bigger? Write it down.
flow.parent: Through the tiny drop the letters usually look about twice as tall. Through the big, flat drop they look almost the same as beside it. Rough answers are fine. The tiny drop shows only part of a letter, so look at one small part, like the round of an o. If it shows nothing clearly, make it a little bigger, about the size of a grain of rice.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar for each drop, as tall as how many times taller it made the letters look.
flow.say: Let's turn the table into a picture. Each drop gets one bar. The taller the bar, the bigger that drop made the letters look.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each drop. Make it as tall as its 'times taller' number.

check.q: In the water-drop test, which drop usually makes the letters look biggest?
options: The big, flat drop
The tiny, round drop
They all magnify the same
check.why: A tiny drop is very curved, almost half a ball. The more curved a lens is, the more sharply it bends light, and the more it magnifies. A big drop spreads out and is nearly flat on top, so it hardly bends the light. Picking the big drop usually means thinking 'more water means more magnifying'. It is the curve that matters, not the amount of water.

flow.do: Ask your child to look at each drop from the side, with their eye level with the ruler.
flow.say: Look at each drop from the side, with your eye level with the ruler. Which one is most like a little ball? Which is flattest?
flow.kid: Look at the drops from the side. Which is roundest? Which is flattest? Does that match your chart?
flow.think: Leeuwenhoek's best microscopes used glass beads smaller than a peppercorn. Why so small?

flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.

What I think: small, round drops magnify more than big, flat drops. What I saw: through the tiny drop, the letters looked about twice as tall, all 3 times. Through the big drop they looked almost the same. Why: the tiny drop is more curved, so it bends the light more.
