experiments.title: The Appearing Coin
experiments.question: Can water make a hidden coin appear, without moving the coin or your eyes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When water is poured into the cup, will the hidden coin stay hidden, or will you see it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep the coin, the cup and your head exactly where they are. Rest your chin on a pile of books so your head does not move. Only change one thing: water or no water.
results_table: Could I see the coin? (yes, no, a little)

materials.item: a steel or clay cup you cannot see through
a one-rupee coin
a small blob of atta dough or clay, to stick the coin down
a jug of water
a pile of books, for your chin

experiments.safety: Water only. Pour slowly so the coin does not move. Wipe up spills.

schedule.what: Hide a coin behind the edge of a cup. Pour in water slowly and watch it appear. Draw why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the cup from the side, with the path of the light from the coin to your eye, with and without water.

flow.do: 1. Stick the coin to the bottom of the cup, near the side, with a little dough. 2. Put the cup on the table. 3. Ask your child to rest their chin on a pile of books and look over the rim.
flow.say: We're going to make a hidden coin appear without touching it. First, stick it down so it can't move.
flow.kid: Stick the coin in the cup with a little dough. Rest your chin on the books. Look into the cup.
flow.context: This is the first step of the appearing-coin test. A coin hidden behind the edge of a cup can be made to appear, just by adding water.

flow.do: Ask your child to slide the books and their head back slowly until the coin just disappears behind the rim. Then stop and keep still.
flow.say: Move back slowly. Stop the moment the coin hides behind the edge of the cup. Now keep your head very still.
flow.kid: Move back slowly until the coin just hides. Stop. Keep your head very still.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess first. 2. Pour water slowly into the cup, down the side away from the coin, until it is nearly full. 3. Your child keeps their head still and watches.
flow.say: I'm going to pour in water. Don't move your head. Tell me what you see.
flow.kid: Keep very still. A grown-up pours water in slowly. Watch the cup. What do you see?
flow.parent: As the water rises, the coin seems to float up into view. If it does not, move back a little further and try again. Some children shout. That is a good result.

check.q: In the appearing-coin test, why did the hidden coin appear when water was poured in?
options: The water lifted the coin up
Light from the coin bent at the water's surface and reached my eye
The water made the coin shiny so it glowed
check.why: The coin was stuck down, so it did not move. Light from it bent as it came out of the water, over the rim and into your eye. Your eye followed the light straight back and saw the coin higher than it is. Picking 'lifted the coin' means trusting the picture, not the coin. Picking 'shiny' mixes up how bright a thing is with where it seems to be.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the cup from the side twice. First empty, with the light from the coin hitting the rim. Then full, with the light bending at the water's surface to reach the eye.
flow.say: Let's draw a model. Draw the light going from the coin to your eye. Without water, what stops it? With water, how does it get to you?
flow.kid: Draw the cup twice. Empty: the light hits the edge. Full: the light bends at the top and reaches your eye.

good: At the top of the water.
Where the water meets the air.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water can make a hidden coin appear by bending its light. What I saw: with no water I could not see the coin. With water, the coin came into view, but it had not moved. Why: light from the coin bends at the top of the water, over the edge of the cup, and into my eye.

experiments.context: This is the appearing-coin test. You hide a coin behind the edge of a cup, keep your head still, and pour in water to make it appear.

activities.title: Look Through Water: three strange things

materials.item: a clear glass or clear plastic bottle, full of water
a paper with a big arrow drawn on it, pointing left
a page of newspaper
a clear plastic ruler or a clear plastic bag, and a spoon of water

activities.safety: Keep the glass in the middle of the table. Wipe up spills.

schedule.what: Look through water at an arrow, a finger and a newspaper. Say what you notice and what you wonder.

activities.record: Draw the strangest thing you saw. Write one thing you wonder about it.

flow.do: 1. Draw a fat arrow pointing left on a paper. 2. Hold it behind the glass of water, close to the glass. 3. Then slowly move the paper back, away from the glass, while your child watches through the glass.
flow.say: Look at this arrow through the glass of water. Keep watching while I move it back. Tell me anything you notice.
flow.kid: Look at the arrow through the glass of water. A grown-up moves it back slowly. Watch the arrow. What happens?
flow.context: This is a quick looking activity at the start of the unit. You look at things through water and notice anything strange, before anyone explains.

good: It flipped round and pointed the other way.
It got wider, then it turned round.

flow.parent: When the arrow is close, it looks wider. Further back, it suddenly flips and points right. The round glass of water is acting like a lens. Do not explain yet. Just enjoy the surprise.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put a finger into the water, at the side of the glass. 2. Look at it from the side.
flow.say: Put your finger in the water. Look at it from the side. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Put your finger in the water. Look from the side. What looks strange?

ask.q: What do you notice about your finger?
good: It looks fatter.
It looks cut off or moved at the top of the water.

flow.do: 1. Lay a clear plastic ruler or a clear plastic bag over a word in the newspaper. 2. Put one small drop of water on the plastic, right over the word, using the tip of a spoon. 3. Look at the word through the drop. 4. Ask: what do you notice, and what do you wonder?
flow.say: Look at this word through the little drop. What do you notice? And what do you wonder?
flow.kid: Put a tiny drop of water on the clear plastic, over a word. Look at the word. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.parent: Write down every 'I wonder' your child says, exactly as they say it. Good wonders: 'Why does water make things big?', 'Why did the arrow flip?', 'Is the water bending something?' Come back to these at the end of the unit and see which ones you can now answer.

check.q: When you looked at a newspaper word through a drop of water, what did you see?
options: The word looked bigger
The word looked smaller
The word disappeared
check.why: A drop of water is round on top, so it bends light like a tiny magnifying glass. The word looks bigger, but it has not changed. If you saw it smaller or vanish, the drop may have been too big and flat, or it may have soaked into the paper. Try a smaller drop on clear plastic.

activities.context: This is a short looking activity to start the unit. You look through water at an arrow, your finger and a newspaper word, and notice what is strange.

activities.title: Magnifier Safari

materials.item: a magnifying glass
small things from home: a leaf from a potted plant, a few grains of sugar and salt, a thread, your fingertip, a piece of cloth, a currency note, and an ant if one comes by
paper and pencil, to draw

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass. Never leave a lens lying in the sunshine, because it can start a fire. Watch ants gently and let them go.

schedule.what: Look at 8 small things through a magnifying glass. Draw 3 of them, without and with the lens.

activities.record: Draw 3 things twice: once as they look to your eye, and once as they look through the lens.

flow.do: 1. Show your child how to hold the lens. Start close to the thing, then lift the lens slowly towards the eye until the picture is sharp. 2. Practise on a fingertip.
flow.say: Hold the lens just above your fingertip. Now lift it slowly towards your eye. Stop when the lines on your finger look big and still sharp.
flow.kid: Hold the lens close to your fingertip. Lift it slowly. Stop when the lines look big and sharp. That is focusing.
flow.context: This is a magnifier safari. You look at tiny things around your home through a magnifying glass, a lens that makes things look bigger.

flow.do: Let your child look at each thing in turn. Try sugar, salt, a leaf, thread, cloth and a currency note. Add an ant if one comes by.
flow.say: Let's go on a safari. Look at each thing. Tell me one thing you can see through the lens that you could not see without it.
flow.kid: Look at each thing through the lens. Find one secret you couldn't see before. Say it out loud.
flow.parent: Things to look for: salt grains are little cubes. Sugar grains are rough blocks. A leaf has a net of tiny veins. Cloth is threads woven over and under. A currency note has very tiny printed letters, called microlettering, that you cannot read without a lens. Your fingertip has ridges. With a strong lens and good light, you may see tiny dots along them. These are pores, the openings where sweat comes out.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw three things twice: as they look to the eye, and as they look through the lens.
flow.say: Choose your three favourite things. Draw each one as it looks with no lens. Then draw it again, as it looked through the lens.
flow.kid: Choose three things. Draw each one twice. Once with no lens. Once through the lens.

check.q: On the magnifier safari, a salt grain looked like a big cube through the lens. What really happened to the salt grain?
options: It grew bigger while the lens was over it
It stayed the same size, only the light from it was bent
It broke into a bigger piece
check.why: The lens bends the light coming from the salt grain, so it reaches your eye as if it came from a big cube. The grain itself does not change. Picking 'it grew' is a very common idea. Lift the lens away and the grain is tiny again at once, so it never grew.

activities.context: This is a safari with a magnifying glass. You look at salt, sugar, leaves, cloth and your fingertip, and find details you cannot see with your eyes alone.

activities.title: Catch the Window: a picture made by a lens

materials.item: a magnifying glass
a sheet of white paper or a white wall
a room with one bright window, in the daytime

activities.safety: Point the lens at the window, never at the Sun. Choose a window with no sunshine coming straight in.

schedule.what: Use a magnifying glass to throw a picture of a window onto paper. Notice which way up it is.

activities.record: Draw the window as it really is, and the picture of it on the paper.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim, with only one bright window uncovered. 2. Stand across the room from the window. 3. Hold the white paper up, facing the window.
flow.say: We're going to catch a picture of the window on this paper, using only a lens. Hold the paper facing the window.
flow.kid: Stand across the room from a bright window. Hold the white paper facing it.
flow.context: This is an activity where you use a magnifying glass to make a picture of a window on a sheet of paper, the way a camera makes a picture.

flow.do: 1. Hold the magnifying glass between the window and the paper, close to the paper. 2. Move it slowly away from the paper, towards the window. 3. Stop when a sharp little picture of the window appears.
flow.say: Hold the lens near the paper. Now move it slowly towards the window. Stop when you see a sharp picture on the paper.
flow.kid: Hold the lens near the paper. Move it slowly away. Stop when a little picture of the window appears.
flow.parent: The picture is usually sharp when the lens is a hand-span or so from the paper. It depends on the lens. If a tree, a building or a passing person is outside, watch for them in the picture. A moving thing outside makes a moving picture.

flow.do: Ask your child to look carefully at the picture, then at the real window.
flow.say: Look at the picture. Then look at the real window. What is different?
flow.kid: Look at the picture. Look at the real window. What is different? Which way up is the picture?

ask.q: What is strange about the picture?
good: It is upside down.
It is small.
Left and right are swapped too.

check.q: When you caught a picture of a bright window on paper with a magnifying glass, which way up was it?
options: The right way up
Upside down
There was no picture, only a blur
check.why: The lens brings light from the top of the window down to the bottom of the picture, and from the bottom up to the top. So the picture is upside down. If you got only a blur, move the lens slowly nearer or further until it is sharp. A camera and your own eye make upside-down pictures in the same way.

activities.context: This activity uses a magnifying glass to throw a small picture of a bright window onto white paper, like a camera does.

activities.title: March Like Light (act it out)

materials.item: a tiled or smooth floor next to a mattress or a thick rug laid flat on the floor
3 to 5 people to hold hands, or 2 toy cars joined by a pencil taped across them
a towel, for the toy car version

activities.safety: Walk slowly and do not pull each other over. Clear the floor of toys first.

schedule.what: Hold hands in a line and march from the floor onto a mattress, straight on and at a slant. Watch the line turn.

activities.record: Draw the line of people from above, before and after the mattress, with arrows showing which way they walked.

flow.do: 1. Stand in a line, side by side, holding hands. 2. Face the mattress straight on. 3. March forward, taking big quick steps on the floor and tiny slow steps once on the mattress.
flow.say: We are a beam of light. On the floor we march fast. On the mattress, which is like water, we march slowly. First, let's march at it straight on.
flow.kid: Hold hands in a line. Face the mattress straight on. March fast on the floor. March slowly on the mattress.
flow.context: This is an act-it-out model of why light bends. People holding hands are the light. The floor is air, where light goes fast. A mattress is water, where light goes slower.

ask.q: Did the line turn when we marched straight on?
good: No, we all slowed down together, so we kept going straight.

flow.do: 1. Go back. This time, face the mattress at a slant, so the person at one end will reach it first. 2. March again: fast on the floor, slow on the mattress. 3. Keep holding hands.
flow.say: Now let's march at the mattress at a slant. The person at this end will reach it first. Watch what happens to our line.
flow.kid: Now march at the mattress at a slant. One end reaches it first. Keep holding hands. What happens to the line?
flow.parent: The first person on the mattress slows down, while the others are still fast. So the line swings round and changes direction. That is exactly how light turns at the edge of water. If you have no helpers, roll two toy cars, joined by a taped pencil, at a slant from the floor onto a towel. The first wheel to hit the towel slows, and the cars turn.

check.q: In the 'march like light' game, why did the line turn when it marched onto the mattress at a slant?
options: One end slowed down first, so the line swung round
The mattress pushed the line sideways
Everyone got tired
check.why: At a slant, the person at one end reaches the slow mattress first and slows down, while the others still march fast. So the line swings round. Light bends for the same reason when it slows down in water. Picking 'pushed sideways' is a common idea, but the mattress only slows people down. It never pushes.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the march from above: the floor, the mattress edge, the line before and after, with arrows.
flow.say: Let's draw a model of what we did, looking down from the ceiling. Where did the line turn?
flow.kid: Draw the march, as if you were a lizard on the ceiling. Draw arrows. Where did the line turn?
flow.think: What do you think would happen if we marched from the mattress back onto the floor, at a slant?

activities.context: This is an act-it-out model of refraction. A line of people marching from a fast floor onto a slow mattress at a slant turns round, just like light turns when it slows down in water.

activities.title: The Bottle Lens and the Flipping Words

materials.item: a smooth, round, clear plastic bottle, full of water, with the lid on
cards with words written in big letters: KID, BOX, CHOICE, and your own name
a clear glass marble, if you have one

activities.safety: Use a plastic bottle, not glass. Never leave a water bottle or marble lying in strong sunshine on paper or cloth. It can focus sunlight and start a fire.

schedule.what: Look at words through a round water bottle. Move them back and see which flip and which do not. Try a marble on a newspaper.

activities.record: Write which words flipped and which looked the same. Draw a word looking wide through the bottle.

flow.do: 1. Lay the bottle on its side on a table. 2. Hold a word card right behind it. 3. Then slowly move the card away.
flow.say: Look at your name through the water bottle. Watch as I move it further away. What happens to the letters?
flow.kid: Lay the bottle down. Look at your name through it. A grown-up moves the card back slowly. What happens?
flow.context: This activity uses a round bottle of water as a lens. You look at words through it and watch them stretch and flip.
flow.parent: Close up, the word looks tall, stretched up and down. Further away, it flips upside down. A bottle lying down bends light only up and down, not side to side. So the letters flip top to bottom, but not left to right.

flow.do: 1. Do the same with the words KID, BOX and CHOICE, written in capital letters. 2. Hold the bottle standing upright this time, and look again.
flow.say: Try the word BOX. Then KID. Which ones look the same when they flip? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Try BOX, KID and CHOICE. Which words look the same after they flip? Try the bottle standing up too.

ask.q: Why does BOX look the same when the bottle flips it?
good: Because B, O and X look the same flipped top to bottom.
The top half and bottom half of those letters match.

flow.parent: With the bottle lying down, it flips words top to bottom. Words like BOX, CHOICE and KID look the same flipped top to bottom, because B, O, X, C, H, I, E, K and D are the same top and bottom. With the bottle standing up, it flips left to right, and other words survive, like TOOT. Let your child explore. This is a puzzle, not a test.

flow.do: Put a glass marble on a newspaper. Look at the words under it from above.
flow.say: This marble is a tiny round lens. Look at the newspaper through it. Is it a stronger or weaker magnifier than the bottle?
flow.kid: Put a marble on the newspaper. Look through it. Does it make letters bigger than the bottle does?

check.q: A round glass marble and a big round water bottle are both lenses. Which one bends light more sharply?
options: The big bottle, because it holds more
The small marble, because it is more curved
Both bend light the same
check.why: A small marble is much more curved than a big bottle, so it bends light more sharply and magnifies more strongly. This matches the water-drop test. Picking 'the big bottle' is the same idea as 'more water, more magnifying'. The curve matters more than the size.

activities.context: This activity uses a round water bottle and a marble as lenses. Words seen through the bottle stretch, then flip upside down, and some words flip without seeming to change.

activities.title: A Galaxy in a Wine Glass: gravity's lens

materials.item: a wine glass, or any glass with a stem and a thick, rounded glass foot. If you have none, skip to the space photos in step 3.
a torch or a phone torch

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the glass. Use a torch, not a candle.

schedule.what: Look at a torch light through the foot of a wine glass and find arcs and rings, like galaxies bent by gravity.

activities.record: Draw the rings and arcs you saw. Write: in space, what bends the light instead of glass?

flow.do: 1. Switch on a torch and lay it on a table, pointing at your child from about two metres away. 2. Hold the glass on its side by the bowl, with the stem pointing at the torch. 3. Your child looks through the middle of the thick foot, along the stem, at the torch.
flow.say: Look at the torch through the bottom of this glass. Now I'll move the glass slowly. Tell me what shapes the light makes.
flow.kid: A grown-up holds the glass. Look at the torch through its thick bottom. Watch the light as the glass moves.
flow.context: This activity uses the thick foot of a wine glass to make shapes like those seen in space, where gravity bends the light of far galaxies.

flow.do: Slowly slide the glass foot sideways across the torch light, and then hold it exactly in line.
flow.say: When the light is exactly behind the middle of the glass, what shape does it make? And when it is a little to one side?
flow.kid: Watch closely. When the light is behind the middle, what shape do you see? And when it is to one side?
flow.parent: Exactly in line, the light spreads into a bright ring. A little to one side, it becomes one or two bright curved arcs. Space telescopes photograph exactly these shapes. They are called Einstein rings and arcs. In space, the 'glass' is the gravity of a huge galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bending light from galaxies far behind it.

good: A ring of light.
Curved lines, like bananas or eyebrows.
Two little lights instead of one.

flow.do: Show your child a photograph of a gravitational lens, for example from the Hubble or James Webb telescope websites, and compare.
flow.say: This is a real photo from a space telescope. The bright arcs are a galaxy far behind. Its light was bent by the gravity of the galaxies in front. Do you see the same shapes as in our glass?
flow.kid: Look at the space photo. Find the bright arcs. Do they look like your glass shapes? In space, gravity bends the light.

check.q: The wine glass bent the torch light into rings and arcs. In space, what bends the light of far galaxies into rings and arcs?
options: Huge glass lenses floating in space
The gravity of huge clusters of galaxies
Clouds of water drops
check.why: In space there is no glass. The gravity of a huge mass, like a cluster of galaxies, bends space itself, so light passing near it curves. Einstein predicted this in 1915. The wine glass only makes a model of the shapes. Picking 'glass lenses' is a fair guess from our model, but the cause in space is different.

activities.context: This activity uses a wine glass foot to make rings and arcs of light, a model of gravitational lenses: places in space where gravity bends the light of far galaxies.

projects.title: Make a Leeuwenhoek Drop Microscope

materials.item: a strip of thin card from a cereal or medicine box, about 10 cm long and 3 cm wide
a small piece of kitchen foil
a sharp pencil, used by a grown-up, to make a small hole in the foil
tape and scissors
water and a toothpick
things to look at: a hair, newspaper print, onion skin, and a drop of water from a flower vase that has stood for a week
a magnifying glass, to compare

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the card and makes the hole in the foil. Look at things near a window or a lamp, never at the Sun. Wash hands after touching old vase water.

schedule.what: Make the drop microscope. Test it on a hair and on newspaper print.
Look at onion skin and a drop of old flower-vase water. Draw what you see and compare it with the magnifying glass.

projects.record: Draw a hair, the onion skin and the vase water as you saw them through the drop. Under each, write which showed more: the tiny drop or the magnifying glass.

flow.do: 1. Cut a hole about 1 cm wide near one end of the card strip. 2. Tape a piece of foil over the hole. 3. Push the sharp pencil point through the middle of the foil, to make a round hole about 2 to 3 millimetres wide.
flow.say: We are going to make a microscope like Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's, about 350 years ago. His lenses were tiny glass beads. Ours will be a tiny drop of water.
flow.kid: A grown-up helps you make a hole in foil on card. Your lens will be a tiny drop of water in that hole.
flow.context: This is the first step of a project to make a tiny microscope from a drop of water, like the one Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used to see tiny living things, about 350 years ago.

flow.do: 1. Dip the toothpick in water. 2. Touch a tiny drop onto the hole in the foil, so the drop sits in the hole. 3. If the drop falls through, make the hole smaller.
flow.say: Now let's place our lens. One tiny drop, sitting in the hole.
flow.kid: Dip a toothpick in water. Put a tiny drop in the foil hole. It should sit there, round and shiny.

flow.do: 1. Sit facing a bright window or a lamp, so light shines through the thing you look at. 2. Hold a hair or a scrap of newspaper under the drop, very close. 3. Bring your eye very close to the drop, from above. 4. Move the hair up and down slowly until it is sharp. 5. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Bring your eye right up to the drop. Move the hair slowly until it looks sharp. How big does it look?
flow.kid: Put your eye right up to the drop. Move the hair slowly until it is sharp. Draw what you see.
flow.parent: The view is small and wobbly, but strongly magnified. A tiny drop may make things look 5 to 10 times bigger. Patience helps. Rest your elbows on the table.

flow.do: 1. Next day, peel a thin skin from inside an onion layer. 2. Lay it under the drop. 3. Then put a drop of old flower-vase water on a clear plastic sheet, and look at it under the drop.
flow.say: Yesterday we tested our microscope. Today let's look at a living thing's skin, from an onion. Can you see small boxes? Those are cells.
flow.kid: Put a thin onion skin under the drop. Look closely. Can you see tiny boxes? Those are called cells.
flow.parent: Onion skin cells look like a wall of tiny bricks. In old vase water, you may see small green specks or moving dots. A water-drop microscope may not show them clearly, so a phone camera held to the drop sometimes helps. Do not worry if they are hard to see. Leeuwenhoek's best glass beads were much stronger than a water drop.

flow.do: Ask your child to compare the drop with the magnifying glass on the same onion skin.
flow.say: Look at the onion skin with the magnifying glass. Then with our drop. Which shows more? Which is easier to use?
flow.kid: Look with the magnifying glass. Then with your drop. Which shows more? Which is easier?

check.q: In the drop microscope project, why did the tiny water drop magnify more than the big magnifying glass?
options: The drop is much more curved, so it bends light more
Water is always better than glass
The drop was closer to the Sun
check.why: A tiny drop is almost a ball, very curved, so it bends light very sharply and magnifies strongly. A big magnifying glass is only gently curved. Leeuwenhoek used tiny beads for the same reason. Picking 'water is better than glass' misses the point, because glass bends light a little more than water does.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a tiny drop of water can work as a strong microscope. What I saw: through the drop, a hair looked as thick as a string, and onion skin looked like tiny bricks. Why: the tiny drop is very round, so it bends light sharply, like Leeuwenhoek's glass beads.

projects.context: This is a two-day project. You make a tiny microscope from a drop of water in a hole in foil, like the one Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used to see tiny living things.

challenges.title: Read the Tiny Print
challenges.problem: Paati has lost her reading spectacles, and the medicine bottle has tiny writing. Your job is to make something that helps her read it, without using a magnifying glass or spectacles.
constraints: You cannot use a magnifying glass, spectacles or a phone camera.
You can only use things you find at home.
It must make the letters look clearly bigger, so Paati can read them.
materials: a page of tiny print, like a medicine label or the small words on a packet
clear plastic bags, cling film, glasses and bottles
general: Put a drop of water on a piece of clear plastic and hold it over the words.
Look through a round glass or bottle of water.
Place a clear glass marble right on the print.
creative: Stretch cling film over the top of a clear glass tumbler. Press the middle down a little and pour a spoon of water into the dip. Put the tiny print under the glass and look down through the water. The curved pool of water works like a lens.
Try a drop of cooking oil instead of water. Oil bends light a little more than water.
Make a tiny pinhole in a card and look at the print through it, very close. It works without bending light at all. Why does it help a little?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own magnifier. Draw it, and test it on the tiny print. Can you read every word now? Is it better than the others?

flow.do: 1. Show your child the tiny print. 2. Read out the challenge and the rules.
flow.say: Here's a real problem. These words are too small for Paati to read. How could you make them look bigger, with no magnifying glass?
flow.kid: These words are tiny. Make them look bigger. You can't use a magnifying glass. Think first.

flow.do: Help your child test the usual ideas: a drop on plastic, a bottle of water, a marble.

challenges.title: Spear the Coin
challenges.problem: A coin lies at the bottom of a bucket of water. Like a fisher with a spear, you must aim a stick at it from one side, then push it in with your eyes closed. Then work out how to aim better.
constraints: You must kneel to one side of the bucket and look at the coin at a slant, not from straight above.
Hold the stick just above the water, pointing along your line of sight, straight at the coin, like a spear. Then close your eyes and push it in the same direction until it touches the bottom.
You get 5 tries with an empty bucket, then 5 tries with water, before you change your way of aiming.
materials: a bucket or a big steel patila, with water about 12 centimetres deep, a little more than half a ruler
a straight stick at least 30 centimetres long, like a 30 centimetre ruler or a long wooden spoon
general: Aim a little below where the coin seems to be, so the stick goes in more steeply. The real coin is deeper than it looks.
Lean over and look from straight above before you aim, then push the stick straight down. Light that comes straight up does not bend.

Put the stick in with your eyes open, and slide it along the bottom until you see it touch the coin. The stick's tip and the coin are at the same depth, so the water moves both pictures in the same way.
creative: Make a 'water telescope': a cut plastic bottle with cling film over one end, pushed just into the water. You now look through a flat, still surface, with no ripples.
Stand a ruler upright in the bucket. Look down at it at a slant and see how the markings under the water look squashed together.
Ask a friend to look from straight above and say 'steeper' or 'flatter' while you aim the stick.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way of aiming. Try it 5 times. Count your hits. Is it better than the others?

flow.do: 1. Put a coin at the bottom of an empty bucket, in the bathroom or on a towel. 2. Ask your child to kneel a step away, to one side. 3. Let them try 5 times. Each time, they point the stick at the coin like a spear and close their eyes. Then they push it in the same direction until it touches the bottom. Count the hits.
flow.say: Here's a fishing challenge. Point the stick at the coin like a spear. Close your eyes and push it in the same direction. How many hits out of 5?
flow.kid: Kneel to one side of the empty bucket. Point the stick at the coin. Close your eyes. Push it in the same direction. Count your hits.
flow.context: This is a challenge like spear fishing. You try to touch a coin at the bottom of a bucket with a stick, first with no water and then with water, and find out why you miss.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into the bucket until it is about 12 centimetres deep. Do not move the coin. 2. Ask your child to guess first: will it be easier or harder now, and why? 3. Let them try 5 more times, from the same place. Count hits.
flow.say: Now there is water over the coin. Will it be easier or harder to hit? Why do you think so? Try 5 times from the same place.
flow.kid: Now the coin is under water. Guess: easier or harder? Try 5 times. Where does the stick land?
flow.parent: Most children hit more often with the empty bucket. With water, the stick usually passes over the coin and lands beyond it, further from them. The coin is deeper than it looks, so a stick aimed at its picture goes over it. If there is no difference, kneel lower, so you look at a bigger slant.

check.q: In Spear the Coin, looking at a slant, where should you aim to hit the coin?
options: Exactly where the coin looks to be
A little below where the coin looks, so the stick goes in more steeply
A little above where the coin looks
check.why: Light from the coin bends as it leaves the water, so you see the coin higher than it really is. The real coin is deeper, below your line of sight. A stick aimed at the picture passes over the real coin. So aim a little below where it looks, as spear fishers do. Even better, look from straight above, where the light does not bend. Picking 'exactly where it looks' means trusting the bent light.

opts: A torch beam bouncing off a steel plate
A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looking broken at the top of the drink
Your hand making a shadow
The Sun getting brighter at noon
quiz.why: Refraction is light bending as it passes from one see-through material into another. The straw looks broken because light from it bends as it leaves the drink. Bouncing is reflection, and a shadow is light being blocked.

quiz.p: Rani, a girl in Class 4, stands in a swimming pool. Her legs look short and bent at the water line. What is true?
opts: Her legs really bend in the water
Light from her legs bends at the surface, so she sees them in the wrong place
The water squeezes her legs
quiz.why: Her legs stay the same. Light from them bends as it leaves the water, and her eyes follow it straight back. So she sees her legs higher and shorter than they are.

quiz.p: Which check shows best that a pencil in water is not really bent?
opts: Look again from the side
Feel along the pencil under the water with a finger
Add more water
quiz.why: Looking from the side again would show the same trick. Touch is not fooled by bending light, so feeling the pencil is a real check.

quiz.p: Thenmozhi wants her water-drop test to be fair. Which one thing should she change from drop to drop?
opts: The size of the drop
The newspaper
Both the ruler and the size of the drop
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If only the drop size changes, any difference in the letters must come from the drop size.

quiz.p: In the water-drop test, why did a tiny round drop make letters look bigger than a big flat puddle did?
opts: It is more curved, so it bends light more
It has more water in it
It sits closer to the ceiling light
quiz.why: The curve decides how strongly a lens bends light. A tiny drop is more curved than a flat puddle, so it magnifies more.

quiz.p: Bhavana looks at a grain of salt through a magnifying glass. Then she puts the lens down. How big is the salt grain now?
opts: Smaller than before
The same size it always was
Still as big as it looked through the lens
quiz.why: The lens never changed the salt grain. It only bent the light coming from it, so the grain looked bigger while she looked through the lens.

quiz.p: Why does a magnifying glass make things look bigger?
opts: It adds extra light to them
It bends the light coming from them
It stretches them
quiz.why: A magnifying glass is a bulging lens. It bends the light from a thing so the light reaches your eye as if from a bigger thing.

quiz.p: After the appearing-coin test, which answer explains it like a scientist?
opts: I think the water lifted the coin.
I think light bends at the water. I saw the coin appear when water was poured in, but the coin was stuck down. So light from the coin bent over the rim to my eye.
It was magic.
quiz.why: A scientist's answer has three parts: what I think, what I saw, and why. The second answer has all three and uses evidence: the coin was stuck down.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT a lens?
opts: A dew drop on a leaf
The glass at the front of a camera
A mirror
The clear lens inside your eye
quiz.why: A mirror bounces light back. It does not bend light passing through it. A dew drop, a camera's glass and your eye's lens all bend light.

quiz.p: Paati, a grandmother, cannot read small print without her reading spectacles. What do the spectacles do?
opts: Bend the light before it enters her eyes, so the picture is sharp
Make the newspaper bigger
Make the room brighter
quiz.why: Spectacles are lenses. They bend light a little before it reaches the eye's own lens, so the picture inside her eye is sharp.

quiz.p: At Kanyakumari, the setting Sun seems to sit on the sea. Where is the real Sun at that moment?
opts: Exactly where it seems to be
Already a little below the horizon, while the air bends its light up to us
Higher up than it seems
quiz.why: The air bends sunlight down around the curve of the Earth, so the Sun looks higher than it really is. We see the Sun for about two minutes after it has set.

quiz.p: A space telescope photographs a far galaxy stretched into an arc. What bent the light from that galaxy?
opts: A giant glass lens in space
The gravity of a huge cluster of galaxies in front of it
Clouds of water in space
quiz.why: Gravity bends light passing near huge masses, as Einstein predicted in 1915. There is no glass in space doing it.

quiz.p: Archerfish spit jets of water at insects sitting above the surface. What have scientists found about their aim?
opts: They always miss, because of the bend
They aim correctly, allowing for the bend in the light
They only spit straight up
quiz.why: The light coming from the insect bends at the surface, so the insect seems to be in the wrong place. Archerfish still hit their target, so they allow for the bend.

applications: Spectacles and contact lenses help hundreds of millions of people read, work and drive.
Phone cameras use several tiny lenses to make sharp photos.
Microscopes let doctors find the germs that cause illnesses like tuberculosis and malaria.
Telescopes use lenses to see the Moon's craters and Jupiter's moons.
Watch repairers and jewellers hold a small lens against one eye to see tiny parts and flaws in gems.
Projectors use lenses to throw a big picture onto a screen.
Eye surgeons in India replace cloudy eye lenses with clear plastic ones in cataract operations.
Lighthouses use huge ringed glass lenses, called Fresnel lenses, to send their beam far out to sea.
Car headlights and torches use lenses to shape their beams.
Binoculars help birdwatchers spot kingfishers across a lake.
Astronomers use gravitational lenses as natural telescopes to see galaxies too far for any glass lens.
Fishers learn to aim below the fish, because of the bend at the water's surface.
Diamond cutters shape stones so light bends and bounces inside them, and they sparkle.

open_questions.q: Exactly how should we describe light's push inside water and glass?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists argued about it for about a hundred years. Many now accept an answer from 2010, but experiments continue and some still disagree.

open_questions.q: Can we ever build a cloak that hides a person from ordinary light?
open_questions.why_open: Cloaks work for microwaves and for tiny things, in some directions. Making one for all colours, all directions and big things may be impossible. Nobody knows yet.

open_questions.q: How do the brains of archerfish and kingfishers learn to deal with the bend?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have shown that archerfish aim correctly, and that they learn by practice. How much is learned and how much they are born with is still being studied.

open_questions.q: What exactly is the dark matter whose gravity bends the light of far galaxies?
open_questions.why_open: Its bending of light shows us where it is. But nobody has ever caught a piece of it, or knows what it is made of.

open_questions.q: Was the Nimrud crystal, about 2,700 years old, really used as a lens?
open_questions.why_open: It does magnify a little. But its shape is uneven, and no writing from the time tells us how it was used.

open_questions.q: Why does my brain trust the bent light, even after I know the pencil is straight?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists who study the mind are still working out how the brain builds what we see, and why knowing does not change it.

maths.problem: In the water-drop test, Kavya looked at a newspaper letter 2 millimetres tall. Through the tiny drop, it looked as tall as 4 millimetres on the ruler beside it. How many times taller did the drop make the letter look?
maths.explain: The letter is really 2 millimetres tall. Through the drop, it looked 4 millimetres tall. 4 divided by 2 is 2. So the drop made the letter look 2 times taller. You can check: 2 + 2 = 4. The letter itself is still 2 millimetres tall.
maths.context: This is about the water-drop test. You put drops of water on a clear ruler lying on newspaper, and compared the letters inside each drop with the letters beside it.
maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'the drop magnifies'. They ask 'how many times bigger?' Dividing one number by the other tells us.

maths.problem: Look at the chart from the water-drop test. Which drop magnified most, and which magnified least?
maths.answer: The tiny drop magnified most, 2 times. The big drop magnified least, only 1 time, which means hardly at all.
maths.explain: The tallest bar is the tiny drop, at 2. The medium drop is at 1 and a half. The big drop is at 1. A bar at 1 means the letters looked just the same size, so that drop hardly magnified.
maths.context: This is about the water-drop test, where drops of different sizes were put on a clear ruler over newspaper, to see which made the letters look biggest.

maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart shows the winner at a glance.

maths.problem: A magnifying glass makes things look 3 times bigger. An ant is 4 millimetres long. How long does the ant look through the lens?
maths.explain: 3 times bigger means 3 lots of the real size. The ant is 4 millimetres long. 3 lots of 4 is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. So the ant looks 12 millimetres long, about as long as your fingernail is wide. The real ant is still 4 millimetres.
maths.context: This is about the magnifier safari, where you looked at small things through a magnifying glass.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying tells us exactly how big the lens makes a thing look, and reminds us the real thing has not changed.

maths.problem: Seen from straight above, water looks about three quarters as deep as it really is. Looking straight down, a temple tank looks 3 metres deep. Is it really shallower than 3 metres, the same, or deeper? About how deep might it be?
maths.explain: If 3 metres is three quarters of the real depth, then each quarter is 1 metre. The whole depth is 4 quarters, so 4 metres. The tank is about 1 metre deeper than it looks. That is why we never jump into water because it looks shallow.
maths.context: This is about the appearing-coin test, where water made a coin at the bottom of a cup look higher than it really was.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let us work out how much the water fools our eyes, which can keep us safe.

maths.problem: In Spear the Coin, Kavya hit the coin 1 time out of 5 when she aimed at the coin's picture. After she learned to look from straight above, she hit it 4 times out of 5. How many more hits did she get?
maths.explain: She got 4 hits the second time and 1 hit the first time. 4 take away 1 is 3. So she got 3 more hits, out of the same 5 tries.

roots.context: We have been learning about refraction, how light bends in water and lenses so things look broken, moved or big. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A pencil in water looks broken at the surface, yet your finger finds it straight. Light from the part under water bends as it leaves the water. Your eyes take the light as if it came straight, so that part looks higher than it is. So we see a thing where its light seems to come from, which is not always where it is.
deep_truth.habit: We assume our eyes show each thing where it is. But eyes only receive light, and they place a thing back along the line the light arrived on. If the light bent on the way, the thing seems moved.
deep_truth.evidence: In the broken-pencil test, the pencil looked most broken from a slant and almost straight from above. Yet it felt straight under the water every time.

three.who_am_i: You see with light that has travelled to you. You can be fooled, and you can check with your hands.
three.what_is_life: Living things carry lenses in their eyes. Kingfishers and archerfish learn to aim in spite of the bend.
three.what_is_this_world: The world reaches you through water, air and glass. Every picture of it has travelled a path to you.

roots.thread: One straight pencil looks broken from the side, almost straight from above, and huge through a lens. Each picture is true to the light that made it, but none of them is the whole pencil. Your finger and the different views, put together, told you what the pencil really is. The world is like this too: one world, met in many ways from many places. We come closer to it by putting the views together.

teachings.teaching: In dim light, a rope can be mistaken for a snake. When we see clearly, the rope was a rope all along. The mistake was in the seeing, not in the rope.
teachings.link: The pencil was straight all along. The 'break' was in the seeing, caused by the bend of the light. Looking from straight above, or touching it, shows what it is.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, from the Buddhist Pali Canon: the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: A king asks several blind men to touch an elephant. One feels the head, one the ear, one the trunk, one the leg. Each says the elephant is only what he felt, and they quarrel. Each felt a real part, but none felt the whole elephant.
teachings.link: From the side, the pencil looks broken. From above, it looks straight. Through a lens, it looks huge. Each view sees part of the truth. Putting views together, as in the broken-pencil test, brings us closer to the whole.

science.text: The air bends light a little. So near the horizon we see the Sun, the Moon and the stars a little higher than they really are. The Sun at sunset is already below the horizon when we see it touch the sea.
Gravity bends light from far galaxies, so astronomers see some galaxies stretched, doubled or in rings, not as they would look without the bend.

other_view.who: The Nyaya school of Indian philosophy, and many scientists today
other_view.view: The world is real, just as it is, and our senses really can know it. The broken pencil is only a mistake of the senses, which we can find and fix by checking. Nothing deeper is hiding behind it. That is an honest view, and it is how science works too.

practice.title: Two ways at once
practice.say: Put your finger into a glass of water and look at it from the side. It looks fat and broken. Now close your eyes. Feel your finger in the water. It feels whole. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, three times. Open your eyes and look again. It still looks broken. But you know it is whole. Just notice both, at the same time, without choosing.
practice.kid: Put your finger in a glass of water. Look. It looks broken. Close your eyes and feel it. It is whole. Breathe slowly three times. Look again, and notice both.

ask: If your eyes can be fooled by water, what else might they be fooling you about?
Is the broken pencil you see 'false', or is it a true picture of the light?
Can two people see the same thing differently, and both be right?
Is the break in the pencil, in the light, or in your eyes?

how_we_found_out.story: Everyone could see that light bends when it goes into water. But why? About 1690, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens said light is a wave, and waves slow down in water. Then they turn, like a line of marchers stepping onto sand. In 1704, Isaac Newton gave a different answer. He said light is a stream of tiny particles, and water pulls them in as they enter. That pull would make light go faster in water, not slower. Newton was so famous that most scientists believed him for about a hundred years. The two ideas made opposite guesses, so a test could decide. But light is so fast that nobody could time it over a short distance. In 1850, in Paris, Léon Foucault built a mirror that spun hundreds of times a second. It let him time light going through a tube of water. The light was slower in water than in air. Hippolyte Fizeau and Louis Breguet found the same that year. Newton's idea of a pull was wrong. Light does slow down in water, and that is why it bends.
how_we_found_out.who: Christiaan Huygens, Isaac Newton, Léon Foucault, and Hippolyte Fizeau with Louis Breguet
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Light speeds up in water, because water pulls its particles in. In 1850, Foucault timed light in water and found it slower, not faster.
